name: Synephrine
lead: Synephrine is a protoalkaloid of the phenethylamine class found chiefly in the immature fruit of the bitter orange, Citrus aurantium. Its main natural form is p-synephrine [1][14]. It is a sympathomimetic compound, and extracts are sold in weight-loss and pre-workout supplements, often as a replacement for ephedra [1][10][12].

The supplement industry markets it for appetite suppression, fat loss and energy. Grokipedia describes clinical evidence for these effects as modest and often involving combination with caffeine [1]. A series of small randomized crossover trials in exercising adults reported that acute p-synephrine ingestion raised the rate of fat oxidation during exercise [3][4][5][6][7]. Whether this translates into long-term fat loss has not been established in the trials cited here.

Safety discussion centres on cardiovascular effects, particularly when bitter orange is combined with caffeine or other stimulants [10][12][11]. Community discussion specific to synephrine is sparse; it appears mostly as an ingredient in energy and fat-burner products.

paras: Synephrine occurs in plants of the Rutaceae family, with the highest levels in unripe bitter orange fruit, and as a trace amine in humans [1]. Analyses of citrus species compared bitter orange with sweet orange, lemon and bergamot [14]. It resembles phenylephrine, a vasopressor used in anaesthesia and intensive care, which is the subject of many unrelated registered trials [15][16]. Researchers have discussed the interaction of related amines with the trace amine-associated receptor 1 [9]. Grokipedia states that p-synephrine acts mainly at alpha-1 adrenergic receptors with weak beta activity, which differs from ephedrine [1].

Randomized crossover trials have tested a single dose of p-synephrine on fat oxidation during exercise. Studies in active adults found a higher fat oxidation rate during cycling [3][4], a similar result in elite cyclists [5], a dose-response relationship across exercise intensities [6], and a study in healthy active women [7]. These measure acute metabolic outcomes during exercise, not body-fat loss over weeks.

Reviews of bitter orange and synephrine in overweight and obesity have examined the clinical and basic research and concluded that it is limited [10][12]; a broader review of obesity supplements also covers the category [2]. A registered comparison of thermogenic supplements on body composition was completed [17], and another trial assessed a pre-workout supplement [18]. Controlled data on safety over long periods are limited.

Grokipedia reports that controlled short-term trials found p-synephrine generally well tolerated in healthy people, while observational reports have linked bitter orange extracts to hypertensive episodes, particularly when combined with other stimulants [1]. Reviews of energy drinks and weight-loss supplements flag stimulant combinations as a source of adverse cardiovascular events [8][11]. Weight-loss supplement use is common among Americans [13].

On T Nation, synephrine appears only incidentally, for example a user logging that they took pills containing it during a diet and felt they were adapting to them as long as they ate [19]. No dedicated looksmaxxing discussion was found.

card.summary: Bitter-orange stimulant sold as the ephedra replacement; small trials show more fat oxidation during exercise, long-term fat loss unproven.
card.aka: Bitter orange, Citrus aurantium extract, p-synephrine
card.note: Cardiovascular concerns, especially stacked with caffeine or other stimulants.

quick.overview:
Synephrine is the main active amine of bitter orange extract, sold in fat burners and pre-workouts as an ephedra-free stimulant.

Small crossover trials found it increases fat oxidation during exercise. Evidence that it produces lasting fat loss is limited, and little forum discussion is dedicated to it.
quick.mechanism: It is a sympathomimetic amine thought to act mainly on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors with weak beta effects, which differs from ephedrine. Acute exercise trials measure higher fat oxidation rates after a dose.
quick.risks: Short controlled trials in healthy adults report good tolerance, while observational reports link bitter orange to blood-pressure and cardiovascular problems, mainly with stimulant stacks. Legal status is as a dietary supplement in the US.
